author: high4
claim: For a sequence of distinct real numbers a_1,...,a_{n^2+1}, if p_i is the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at a_i and q_i is the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at a_i, then the ordered pairs (p_i,q_i) are pairwise distinct. Consequently, if every p_i and q_i were at most n, there could be at most n^2 positions.
evidence: Fix i<j. Since the terms are distinct real numbers, exactly one of a_i<a_j or a_i>a_j holds. In the first case, append a_j to a strictly increasing subsequence of length p_i ending at a_i; this gives p_j>=p_i+1. In the second case, append a_j to a strictly decreasing subsequence of length q_i ending at a_i; this gives q_j>=q_i+1. Thus (p_i,q_i)!=(p_j,q_j) for every i<j. If all coordinates belonged to {1,...,n}, there would be only n^2 possible ordered pairs, so n^2+1 positions are impossible.

links.statement: The endpoint-length pairs are injective, yielding the target theorem by pigeonhole.

glossary.a_i: the real number in position i of the given sequence
glossary.p_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence of the given sequence that ends at position i
glossary.q_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence of the given sequence that ends at position i

author: high3
claim: For each position i, let p_i be the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i and q_i the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i. If no required subsequence has length n+1, then all pairs (p_i,q_i) lie in {1,...,n}^2 and are pairwise distinct.
evidence: Assume every strictly increasing and strictly decreasing subsequence has length at most n. The singleton at i gives 1<=p_i,q_i<=n. For i<j, distinctness of the real entries gives either x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j. In the first case, append x_j to a longest increasing subsequence ending at i, obtaining p_j>=p_i+1, so p_j differs from p_i. In the second case, append x_j to a longest decreasing subsequence ending at i, obtaining q_j>=q_i+1, so q_j differs from q_i. Thus (p_i,q_i)!=(p_j,q_j). This is a by-definition/logical derivation, confidence 1.0, non-fragile; no counterexample follow-up is needed.

links.statement: The endpoint-rank pairs are bounded and pairwise distinct under the negation of the target conclusion.

glossary.x_i: the real number in position i of the given sequence
glossary.p_i: maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.q_i: maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i

author: high6
claim: For a finite sequence of distinct real numbers, assign to each index i the pair (p_i,q_i), where p_i is the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at i and q_i is the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at i. Then the pairs (p_i,q_i) are pairwise distinct.
evidence: If i<j, distinctness of the terms gives either x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j. In the first case, append x_j to a strictly increasing subsequence of length p_i ending at x_i, obtaining p_j>=p_i+1, so p_j differs from p_i. In the second case, append x_j to a strictly decreasing subsequence of length q_i ending at x_i, obtaining q_j>=q_i+1, so q_j differs from q_i. Thus the endpoint-rank pairs at i and j differ for every i<j.

links.statement: The endpoint-rank map i ↦ (p_i,q_i) is injective.

glossary.x_i: the real number at index i in the sequence
glossary.p_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose last term is x_i
glossary.q_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence whose last term is x_i
glossary.j: a later index in the sequence

author: high
claim: For a sequence x_1,...,x_m of distinct real numbers, let p_i and q_i be the maximum lengths of, respectively, a strictly increasing and a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i. Then the ordered pairs (p_i,q_i) are pairwise distinct.
evidence: Fix indices i<j. Since x_i and x_j are distinct real numbers, either x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j. If x_i<x_j, take a strictly increasing subsequence of length p_i ending at x_i and append x_j; all of its indices remain increasing and its values are strictly increasing, so it is a strictly increasing subsequence of length p_i+1 ending at x_j. Hence p_j>=p_i+1. If x_i>x_j, the same argument with a strictly decreasing subsequence gives q_j>=q_i+1. In either case (p_i,q_i)!=(p_j,q_j). As every two distinct indices have an earlier and a later one, all pairs are pairwise distinct.

glossary.m: the length of the finite sequence
glossary.x_i: the real number in position i of the sequence
glossary.p_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.q_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i

author: high7
claim: Pair-label reformulation: for a sequence a_1,...,a_{n^2+1} of distinct real numbers, if I_i and D_i are the maximum lengths of strictly increasing and strictly decreasing subsequences ending at position i, respectively, then all pairs (I_i,D_i) are distinct. Consequently, if no such subsequence has length n+1, the n^2+1 positions would inject into the n^2-element set {1,...,n}^2, which is impossible.
evidence: Fix i<j. Since a_i and a_j are distinct, either a_i<a_j or a_i>a_j. In the first case, append a_j to a longest increasing subsequence ending at i, obtaining I_j>=I_i+1, so (I_i,D_i)!=(I_j,D_j). In the second case, append a_j to a longest decreasing subsequence ending at i, obtaining D_j>=D_i+1, again making the pairs unequal. Thus every two positions have different labels. If neither requested subsequence exists, by definition 1<=I_i<=n and 1<=D_i<=n for every i. There are only n^2 possible labels, contradicting the n^2+1 pairwise distinct labels.

glossary.a_i: the real number in position i of the given sequence
glossary.I_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.D_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i

author: high2
claim: Let x_1,...,x_m be pairwise distinct real numbers. For each position i, let I_i be the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at x_i and let D_i be the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at x_i. Then the ordered pairs (I_i,D_i) are pairwise distinct.
evidence: Take positions i<j. Since x_i and x_j are distinct, either x_i<x_j or x_i>x_j. If x_i<x_j, append x_j to an increasing subsequence of length I_i ending at x_i; this gives an increasing subsequence ending at x_j of length I_i+1, so I_j>=I_i+1 and therefore I_j differs from I_i. If x_i>x_j, the same append argument for decreasing subsequences gives D_j>=D_i+1, so D_j differs from D_i. Thus (I_i,D_i) differs from (I_j,D_j) for every i<j.

links.statement: Terminal increasing/decreasing ranks give an injective map from positions to ordered pairs.

glossary.m: The length of the finite sequence.
glossary.x_i: The real number in position i of the sequence.
glossary.I_i: The maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose last term is x_i.
glossary.D_i: The maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence whose last term is x_i.

author: high5
claim: The target theorem follows from injectivity of the endpoint rank pairs: for each term, pair the maximum lengths of an increasing and a decreasing subsequence ending at that term; if both lengths are at most n, these pairs cannot repeat, yet only n^2 pairs are available.
evidence: Let a_1,...,a_{n^2+1} be the sequence. For each i, let I_i be the largest length of a strictly increasing subsequence whose final term is a_i, and let D_i be the analogous largest length for strictly decreasing subsequences. These maxima exist because the singleton a_i is an eligible subsequence and there are finitely many index subsequences ending at i. Suppose the desired conclusion fails. Then 1<=I_i<=n and 1<=D_i<=n for every i. Hence each (I_i,D_i) belongs to the n^2-element set {1,...,n}x{1,...,n}. By the pigeonhole principle, two indices i<j have (I_i,D_i)=(I_j,D_j). Since the sequence terms are distinct, either a_i<a_j or a_i>a_j. If a_i<a_j, take an increasing subsequence of length I_i ending at a_i and append a_j; this is an increasing subsequence of length I_i+1 ending at a_j, so I_j>=I_i+1, contradicting I_i=I_j. If a_i>a_j, the same append argument for a decreasing subsequence gives D_j>=D_i+1, contradicting D_i=D_j. Thus the failure assumption is impossible.

links.statement: Endpoint rank-pair injectivity proves the target theorem.

glossary.n: the positive integer in the target theorem
glossary.a_i: the real number in position i of the given sequence
glossary.I_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.D_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i
